name: strace
one_line: trace the system calls of a program
plain: A program cannot do much by itself: to open a file, read the network or start another program it must ask the operating system, using system calls. `strace` shows each of those requests as it happens, with the arguments and the result.

That makes it a flashlight for mystery binaries: which files does it open, which config does it read, which server does it connect to, what does it compare your input against? You do not need the source code.
when: See which files and libraries a program opens (and which ones fail).
Find out why a program fails with a vague error.
Watch a crackme call strcmp-like functions or read a flag file.
See network connections and exec calls a program makes.
Get a quick count of which system calls take the time.

examples.title: Trace a command
examples.explain: Prints every system call: execve, openat, read, write, close... Lines with -1 ENOENT mean a file was not found.

examples.title: Save the trace to a file
examples.explain: -o writes the trace to a file so you can grep it; the program's own output stays on screen.

examples.title: Only file-related calls
examples.explain: -e trace=file shows only calls that use file names (open, stat, access...). Other groups: network, process, memory, signal.

examples.title: Only some calls
examples.explain: Names the calls you want to see.

examples.title: Follow child processes
examples.explain: -f follows forks and threads. A program that starts another program is traced through it.

examples.title: Show long strings
examples.explain: By default strings are cut at 32 characters; -s raises the limit so you can read the whole path or password check.

examples.title: Count instead of listing
examples.explain: -c prints a summary table at the end: how many times each call ran and where the time went.

examples.title: Attach to a running process
examples.explain: -p attaches to a process id. Needs the right permissions.

examples.title: Timestamps and durations
examples.explain: -tt prefixes wall-clock time, -T appends the time spent in each call.

examples.title: Find the secret it compares
examples.explain: Look at what it reads after you type input: the comparison data sometimes appears in a read or write.

mistakes: Reading all output: filter with -e trace=file or grep the -o file.
Forgetting -f and missing the real work done in a child process.
Truncated strings hiding the password: use -s 200.
Running strace on a setuid program and expecting it to keep privileges: it will not.
Mixing up strace (system calls) with ltrace (library calls).
try: Run strace -e trace=file cat /etc/hostname and name each file it opens.
Trace a small crackme with -s 100 and find where it reads your input.
Use -c on ls -R / and see which call costs the most.
see_also: ltrace(1), gdb(1), ldd(1), lsof(8), perf(1), and the system-call list in syscalls(2).
captured_with: Examples are written to explain a technique; they are not captured output.
